pr_body:
This PR introduces a new Elasticsearch command line tool that can serve as a readiness probe client. To determine if Elasticsearch is up we establish a socket connection to the HTTP port Elasticsearch serves requests. The client will only connect to the socket, it will not attempt to establish any communication, essentially it checks if the port is open and ready.

With this implementation we achieve the requirements for https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/81168 without any new open ports, without worrying about SSL or authentication.

Closes [#81168](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/81168)

review_comment: I don't think this is sufficient as a readiness check. The port is opened async to when the node is ready to accept api requests (eg recoveries etc happen). This is why tests wait for green before running.

I consulted on this with the distributed team. My initial thought was the same, waiting for green (or yellow) before we claim we are up and running, but that would cause issues on master failover/restart, making the whole cluster appear down. Initially @DaveCTurner suggested we monitor cluster state and wait for the following condition:

```
ClusterChangedEvent.state().blocks().hasGlobalBlock(GatewayService.STATE_NOT_RECOVERED_BLOCK) == false
```

Meaning we have sufficiently recovered cluster state to claim the node is up. I believe the ports open after this happens during bootstrap.

After my initial prototype of checking for the cluster state event change, there was a high bandwidth discussion between @tbrooks8, @henningandersen and @DaveCTurner and they recommended this approach going forward.

I suppose we may need to clear-up the exact requirement, are we looking for 'green' node or just node that can respond to requests?

My earlier prototype (of just the server part) that listens on cluster change events is here: https://github.com/grcevski/elasticsearch/tree/feature/readiness_check

If a port being open is all we are looking for, then I don't see why a custom tool is needed, it seems possible to do a TCP probe in kubernetes?
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/#define-a-tcp-liveness-probe
Oh, I didn't know you could do TCP probes, I thought it was HTTP and call program only. Then this PR makes no sense. I'll follow-up on the issue with this resolution.
